story: Ad hoc. Made for one particular purpose only, not planned in advance. One monsoon night, water rushed into the ground floor of a hospital in Sylhet. There was no plan for this, so nurses, cleaners and patients' relatives formed an ad hoc team on the spot, passing beds and medicine boxes up the stairs, hand to hand. By morning the job was done, and the team simply melted away. Ad hoc is Latin for "for this": for this one job only. So, what do you call a team put together on the spot for a single task? ... Ad hoc.

Allow. To permit, and also to admit that something is true. Rafi and his grandfather argued all through dinner about whose generation had it harder. Grandfather spoke of walking to school through knee-deep mud; Rafi spoke of Dhaka traffic. At last the old man [chuckle] put down his tea. "I will allow that your traffic is worse than my mud." Rafi [laugh] grinned and allowed that the mud sounded terrible too. When you allow a point into the argument, you admit it is true. So, what verb means to admit that the other side has a point? ... Allow.

Appropriate. As an adjective, suitable for the situation. As a verb, to take something for your own use, often without permission. Mahin spent a month painting a poster for his university's Pohela Boishakh festival. A week later, a senior student hung it in the hall with his own name at the bottom. Mahin felt his face burn. The senior had appropriated his work, and it was hardly appropriate behaviour. Inside appropriate hides the root of property, meaning your own: to appropriate is to make something your property. So, what verb means to take someone else's work as your own? ... Appropriate.

August. Respected and impressive; majestic. On convocation day, an eighty-year-old professor walked onto the stage in his black gown, white-haired and perfectly upright. Two thousand graduates rose to their feet, and even the noisy photographers fell silent. Shirin felt a shiver of pride just to be in that august hall, before such an august figure. Think of Augustus, the Roman emperor whose very title meant the revered one; an august person carries that same grandeur. So, what word describes a presence so dignified that a whole hall stands in silence? ... August.

Base. Shamefully dishonourable and selfish, without moral decency. During a flood in Sunamganj, one shopkeeper locked away his rice and sold it to hungry families at three times the normal price. When a relief volunteer begged him to be fair, he only raised the price again. The villagers were disgusted. Of all the things they saw that year, his greed was the most base. Picture the lowest floor of a building: a base act sinks to the very bottom of human behaviour. So, what word describes cheating desperate people for profit? ... Base.

Champion. To publicly support or fight for a cause. When the council planned to fill in an old pond in Mymensingh to build a market, a retired schoolteacher named Rumana refused to stay quiet. She wrote to newspapers, gathered her former students, and spoke at every public meeting. When the plan was finally dropped, Rumana [laugh] hugged the children who had marched with her. She had championed the pond. The trick: a sports champion wins for himself, but when you champion a cause, you fight for something beyond yourself. So, what verb means to stand up publicly for a cause? ... Champion.

Contemporary. Belonging to the same period as someone else; also, of the present day. In nineteen thirty, Rabindranath Tagore sat with Albert Einstein near Berlin and talked about truth and reality. Ishita read about it for her history class and was amazed. The poet she grew up reciting and the scientist from her physics book were contemporaries, alive at the same time. Today the word can also mean modern, as in contemporary art. Con means with, and tempus means time: with the same time. So, what word describes two people who lived in the same era? ... Contemporary.

Content. Peacefully satisfied. Rahim rows a wooden boat on the Meghna. Each evening he sits outside his tin-roofed house with a cup of sweet tea, [sigh] watching the sky turn orange over the water. When a visitor from Dhaka asked whether he wanted more from life, Rahim smiled, [chuckle] and shook his head. "I have enough." He was truly content. Content is the root of contentment; do not mix it up with the content of a book, which is what the book contains. So, what word describes someone peacefully satisfied with what they have? ... Content.

Conventional. Following accepted customs and standards; traditional. At a family dinner, Zayan's parents discussed his future: doctor, engineer, or a government job. Safe, respected, conventional. Then Zayan quietly said he wanted to photograph tigers in the Sundarbans. The table went silent, and his mother slowly put down her spoon. A convention is a meeting where people come to an agreement, so the conventional path is the one everyone has already agreed on. So, what word describes the safe, traditional path that everyone expects you to take? ... Conventional.

Discount. To regard something as unimportant or untrustworthy, and set it aside. When a neighbour told Mitu's grandmother that bitter gourd juice could replace her insulin, Mitu felt a flash of worry. But the doctor gently discounted the advice and kept her grandmother on her medicine. After that, Mitu learned to discount the miracle cures forwarded in family chats. The trick: in a shop, a discount cuts the price; in an argument, discounting a claim cuts its value to almost nothing. So, what verb means to dismiss a claim as not worth trusting? ... Discount.

Documentary. Based on real documents and records. For years, Tanvir's family argued over who owned a small plot of land in Cumilla. Every uncle had a story, but stories proved nothing. Then Tanvir opened his great-grandfather's old tin trunk and found the deed, the paper brown and brittle, the seal still clear. His aunt [gasp] pressed a hand to her mouth. At last there was documentary proof. The word has document right inside it: documentary evidence is evidence written down on paper. So, what kind of evidence rests on written records rather than memory? ... Documentary.

Economy. Using money, effort or words carefully, without waste. Sara's mother runs a family of five on one small salary. She buys vegetables in season, measures cooking oil by the spoon, and turns last night's rice into panta for breakfast. Nothing is ever wasted. Years later, Sara writes her essays the same way, with an economy of words that her teacher praises. Think of economy class on a plane: no extra space, nothing wasted. So, what word means careful use of money, effort or words, with nothing wasted? ... Economy.

Elementary. Basic; belonging to the simplest beginning stages. On the first day of his GRE quant course, Arif felt almost insulted. The teacher started with fractions, percentages and the area of a triangle, things he had learned in class six. Then his first practice test came back, and he had missed four elementary questions. [sigh] He stopped complaining and started practising. Elementary comes from element, the basic building block of everything. So, what word describes the simplest, most basic ideas a subject begins with? ... Elementary.

Entitled. Feeling owed special treatment you have not earned. At the university canteen, students waited in a long line for lunch. A boy in designer sunglasses walked straight to the front and said, "Do you know who my father is?" The cashier calmly pointed to the back of the line, and a few students quietly cheered. He was entitled, acting as if rules were only for other people. Picture him wearing an invisible royal title: an entitled person behaves like a lord without ever earning the crown. So, what word describes someone who expects privileges they never earned? ... Entitled.

Facility. A natural ease or skill in doing something. Joya's little brother has never had a single music lesson, yet he can hear a song once on the radio and play it on the harmonium straight away. His fingers find the notes as if they already knew them. When he finishes, the whole family [laugh] claps and cheers. Everyone notices his facility with melody. Facility shares its Latin root with facile and facilitate, all from the word for easy, so a facility is a skill that comes easily. So, what word means a natural ease at doing something? ... Facility.

Frank. Open, honest and direct. Shuvo nervously handed his first short story to his mentor, hoping for praise. She read it, put down her tea, and said, "The opening is dull, and the ending is borrowed. But the third page is brilliant. Build from there." It stung, yet Shuvo walked home grateful. She had been frank with him, and her frank words helped more than any polite ones. The trick: the old French word franc meant free, so frank speech is free of disguise. So, what word describes feedback that is open, honest and direct? ... Frank.

Minute. Extremely small; also, precise and detailed. In a weaving village near Narayanganj, Lamia watched an old Jamdani weaver lift threads one by one, working a minute flower into the cloth. Each petal was smaller than a grain of rice. One sari can take him months of such minute work, and Lamia could hardly breathe as she watched. Unlike the minute on a clock, this minute is about size, and it shares its root with diminish and minuscule, both about smallness. So, what word describes detail so tiny you must lean close to see it? ... Minute.

Noble. Having high moral qualities; also, aristocratic. A rickshaw puller in Dhaka found a bag under his seat holding two lakh taka. He had rent to pay and a daughter who needed school fees. Still, he spent the whole day searching until he found the owner, returned every note, and refused a reward. People who read the story felt their throats tighten. It was noble, nobler than any title. The trick: noble is the opposite of base; base sinks low, noble rises high. So, what word describes an act of high moral character, like returning money you badly need? ... Noble.

Plastic. Easily shaped or moulded; flexible and adaptable. Priya's little son moved from Sylhet to Dhaka at four. Within months he was chattering in a new accent, picking up words from cousins and cartoons. Priya worried, but her neighbour, a doctor, smiled and said, "A child's brain is plastic. It reshapes itself as it learns." The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to mould, which is also how the material plastic got its name. Think of soft clay in a potter's hands. So, what word describes something that can be easily shaped and reshaped? ... Plastic.

Prime. To prepare someone or something for action. In the last week before Tania's GRE, her tutor taught her nothing new. Instead, every morning at nine, the exact hour of her real test, he handed her a timed practice set, so her mind would wake up sharp at that time. He was priming her for the big day. It is just like a painter in Old Dhaka priming a wall with a base coat before the real colour goes on. So, what verb means to get someone ready for action? ... Prime.

Radical. Favouring drastic change; also, relating to the very roots of something. For years, a village in Kurigram fought floods with small fixes: sandbags, higher plinths, new drains. Every monsoon, the water won. Then a young engineer named Farhan made a radical proposal: build homes on floating platforms that rise with the water. The elders [gasp] stared at him in disbelief. Radical comes from the Latin radix, meaning root, so radical change goes all the way down to the roots. So, what word describes change that is drastic and fundamental? ... Radical.

Reflect. To think carefully about something; also, to show or express it. After failing her first GRE practice test, Sumaiya looked at the score, [sigh] and did not rush into another one. She sat by her hostel window with the report and reflected. Which questions had she rushed? Which words had she only guessed? Three months later, her final score reflected all that patient work. Think of a mirror: it reflects your face, and when you reflect, you turn your thoughts back on yourself. So, what verb means to think deeply, or to show something clearly? ... Reflect.

Remarkable. Unusual enough to be noticed and admired; exceptional. Anika's neighbour sold vegetables in Karwan Bazar for thirty years, waking before dawn in every season. Alone, she raised four children and sent all four to university. On the day her youngest became a doctor, the whole lane came out to congratulate her, and Anika cried a little too. Everyone agreed her life was remarkable. The word is simply remark plus able: something remarkable is worth remarking on. So, what word describes an achievement so exceptional that people cannot stop talking about it? ... Remarkable.

Remote. Far away and distant; also, slight or faint, as in a remote chance. Sabbir's grandparents live on a remote char in the middle of the Jamuna, reachable only by boat. One stormy evening, Sabbir asked the old boatman whether the ferry would still run. The boatman looked at the black sky and the churning water. [sigh] "Only a remote chance, son." Think of a remote control: it works from far away, and a remote chance is just as far from happening. So, what word means far away, or so slight it hardly exists? ... Remote.

Slight. As an adjective, small or minor. As a verb, to insult someone by ignoring them; as a noun, the insult itself. At a cousin's wedding in Chattogram, the host greeted every guest with hugs. When Nadia's mother reached the gate, he looked past her and turned to the next guest. She smiled politely, but Nadia saw her hands tremble. It was no slight mistake; it was a slight. The trick: to slight someone is to treat them as slight, too small to notice. So, what verb means to insult someone by treating them as not worth noticing? ... Slight.

Sound. Based on valid reasoning; also, in good condition and reliable. When Imran told his parents he wanted to study in Germany, his father frowned. Then Imran laid out his plan: savings for the first year, a partial scholarship, a part-time job already arranged, and a clear career goal. His father read it twice, [chuckle] then nodded. "Your reasoning is sound." Think of the phrase safe and sound: a sound argument is whole and solid, with no cracks in it. So, what word describes reasoning that is solid and reliable? ... Sound.

Stem from. To come from, or to be caused by. Nusrat's little sister would never go near the pond behind their village home, even on the hottest days. One evening their mother explained that the fear stemmed from an old accident: at three, the girl had slipped off a boat and been pulled out just in time. Now Nusrat understood, and she held her sister's hand a little tighter. Picture a plant: its stem grows from hidden roots, just as a problem can stem from a hidden cause. So, what phrase means to originate from something? ... Stem from.

Suspect. Not to be trusted; of doubtful quality. A website promised Shakil a full scholarship abroad if he paid a ten thousand taka fee within twenty-four hours. The page was full of spelling mistakes, gave no office address, and listed a phone number nobody answered. His professor took one look and said, "This offer is suspect." Shakil [gasp] realised how close he had come to paying. Usually a suspect is a person the police doubt; here the word describes anything that deserves the same doubt. So, what word describes an offer or a claim that cannot be trusted? ... Suspect.

Universal. Done by or relating to everyone; true in all cases. At the start of each school year, children across Bangladesh, in city schools and on river islands alike, receive brand-new free textbooks. Kamal still remembers the smell of fresh paper and ink the morning his daughter came home hugging hers. The goal behind it is universal education: every child, with no exceptions. Universal comes from universe, everything that exists, so a universal rule leaves no one out. So, what word describes something that applies to everyone, everywhere? ... Universal.

Wanting. Lacking; not good enough. Nayeem spent weeks on his first research paper and handed it in proudly. It came back with one line in red ink: "The analysis is wanting." For a moment he thought his professor simply wanted more of it. [chuckle] Then he understood that his analysis fell short, [sigh] and he opened his laptop again. In older English, want meant lack, as in the saying "for want of a nail, the shoe was lost." So, what word describes work that is lacking, not good enough? ... Wanting.
